title: Pluralistic Leaderboards
claim: Our committee selection stays stable across heterogeneity regimes, whereas the standard top-k scoring baseline and a naive heuristic baseline exceed the stability threshold.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, shared legend in right panel, dashed threshold line
description: Three line plots in a row. Each shows stability approximation factor (y-axis) against committee size k, from 1 to 18 (x-axis). The panels are titled 'Committee stability' with phi = 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9, the Mallows dispersion parameter. Each panel has three series with shaded standard-error bands. Blue circles are Bradley-Terry top-k, green stars are Mallows centers, and orange crosses are the Algorithm 1 committee. A dashed grey horizontal line at 1.0 marks the stability threshold. At phi = 0.1, Bradley-Terry goes well above 1 and the others stay below it. At phi = 0.9, the Mallows centers rise above the threshold while Algorithm 1 stays below 1. The legend sits inside the right panel. The eye goes first to the blue curve and the dashed threshold line.
caption: Comparison on mixtures of Mallows of the stability of committees produced by Algorithm 1 and the two described baseline methods. For each k, a mixture of Mallows model is created with k central rankings sampled uniformly at random, and a committee of size k is produced by each method. Values of ˆγ ≤1 indicate that the committee produced was stable. The plotted points and error regions show the mean and standard error, respectively, after 10 repeats.
abstract: Recent leaderboard-based evaluations of large language models aggregate user feedback by fitting a Bradley--Terry model to pairwise comparisons, producing a single global ranking based on a latent quality score. While appealing for its simplicity, this approach is incompatible with heterogeneous preferences: when LLMs are used across diverse tasks and use cases, users who favor fundamentally different model behaviors can be systematically misrepresented when collapsed into a single quality score. To address this issue, we study \emph{pluralistic leaderboards} that aim to remain \emph{stable} with respect to heterogeneous user populations. Drawing on ideas from social choice theory, we adapt the notion of \emph{local stability}, which requires that no model outside the top-$k$ positions is collectively preferred to the top-$k$ set by more than $O(1/k)$ fraction of users. Building on techniques from the social choice literature, we design an alternative leaderboard mechanism that satisfies local stability while eliciting only $\widetilde{O}(k)$ pairwise comparisons per user, where $k$ is the size of the prefix for which stability is guaranteed. Using data from LMArena, we show that standard Bradley--Terry aggregation can violate local stability in practice, whereas our method provides substantially stronger stability guarantees.
